title: Block Placement Queries
statement:
Picture a number line that starts at `0` and runs forever to the right. You process `queries` in order, and each query is one of:

- `[1, x]`: put an obstacle at position `x`. No obstacle stands at `x` before this query.
- `[2, x, sz]`: decide whether a block of length `sz` could sit somewhere on the line with both of its ends inside `[0, x]` and no obstacle strictly inside it. Its ends may touch obstacles. Nothing is actually placed, so these queries change nothing.

Return a list of booleans with one answer per type-2 query, in the order those queries appear: `true` if the block fits, `false` if it does not. At least one query has type 2.
constraints: A type-1 query is [1, x] and a type-2 query is [2, x, sz]
A type-1 query never builds where an obstacle already stands
At least one query has type 2
notes:
## Intuition

For a type-2 query only obstacles up to `x` matter. With the origin, they cut `[0, x]` into pieces: from `0` to the first obstacle, between neighbours, and from the last obstacle to `x`. The block fits exactly when the longest piece is at least `sz`. Rescanning every obstacle per query is the O(q²) brute force.

A segment tree over the positions does better. Each node stores the `first` and `last` obstacle in its range and the widest `gap` between neighbouring obstacles inside it. Two halves combine easily: the only new gap runs from the left half's last obstacle to the right half's first.

## Approach

1. `limit` is the largest position in any query. The arrays `first`, `last` (`-1` when a range has no obstacle) and `gap` are indexed by tree node.
2. Type 1: `update` walks down to leaf `x`, marks it, and on the way back up rebuilds each node from its children `left` and `right`.
3. Type 2: reset `prev = 0` (the origin) and `best = 0`, then `scan` the nodes covering `[0, x]` from left to right. Each covered node with obstacles offers its inner `gap` and the piece `first[node] - prev`; then `prev` moves to its `last` obstacle.
4. Push whether `Math.max(best, x - prev) >= sz`, where `x - prev` is the final piece.

## Example 1, step by step

`queries = [[1,2],[2,3,3],[2,3,1],[2,2,2]]`, so `limit = 3`.

- `[1,2]`: the leaf for 2 and every node above it get `first = last = 2`.
- `[2,3,3]`: the scan meets obstacle 2, so `best = 2 - 0 = 2` and `prev = 2`; the final piece is `3 - 2 = 1`. `2 < 3`: `false`.
- `[2,3,1]`: same pieces; `2 >= 1`: `true`.
- `[2,2,2]`: `best = 2`, `prev = 2`, final piece `0`; `2 >= 2`: `true`.

Result: `[false, true, true]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(X + q log X) for X = `limit`: O(X) to fill the arrays, then O(log X) nodes per update or scan.
- Space: O(X) for the three arrays of about `4X` entries.

## Pitfalls

- Ends may touch obstacles and `x`: compare with `>=`, not `>`.
- The piece crossing `x` counts only up to `x`, not up to the next obstacle.
- The origin acts as an obstacle: the first piece starts at `0`.
- `scan` must visit the left child first, or `prev` pairs obstacles that are not neighbours.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `limit` | largest position in any query |
| `first`, `last` | first and last obstacle in a node's range, `-1` if none |
| `gap` | widest gap between neighbouring obstacles inside a node's range |
| `node`, `lo`, `hi`, `mid` | a tree node, its range, and the split point |
| `left`, `right` | the node's children |
| `pos` | position becoming an obstacle |
| `prev` | last obstacle the scan passed, starting at the origin |
| `best` | widest piece the scan found |
| `results` | answers to the type-2 queries |
| `type`, `x`, `sz` | fields of one query |

narration.2: Every position is at most the largest x in the queries, so the tree covers 0..limit.
narration.3: first[node] is the leftmost obstacle in the node's range, or -1 when the range has none.
narration.4: last[node] is the rightmost obstacle in the node's range.
narration.5: gap[node] is the widest distance between neighbouring obstacles inside the range.
narration.7: update turns pos into an obstacle and repairs every node above it.
narration.8: A leaf covers the single position pos.
narration.9: It now holds one obstacle, which is both its first and its last.
narration.16: Go down into the half that contains pos.
narration.21: The range's first obstacle is the left half's first, if the left half has any.
narration.22: Its last obstacle is the right half's last, if the right half has any.
narration.23: Gaps inside either half are still gaps of the whole range.
narration.24: When both halves hold obstacles, one more gap joins them...
narration.25: ...running from the left half's last obstacle to the right half's first.
narration.31: scan visits the nodes that cover [0, x], from left to right.
narration.32: Skip ranges that start past x and ranges with no obstacles.
narration.35: This node lies fully inside [0, x], so take it as a whole.
narration.36: Its inner gaps and the piece from the previous obstacle to its first one are candidates.
narration.37: Its last obstacle becomes the previous obstacle for the nodes further right.
narration.41: Visit the left half first so that obstacles are met in increasing order.
narration.46: Handle the queries in their given order.
narration.48: Type 1 builds an obstacle at x.
narration.50: Type 2 starts its scan at the origin, which acts like an obstacle.
narration.52: Find the widest piece between obstacles up to x.
narration.53: The final piece runs from the last obstacle to x; the block fits if some piece is at least sz.
narration.56: Return one answer per type-2 query.
